slides.title: How Nature Works in Harmony
slides.subtitle: A train rolls over an elephant corridor while a herd passes safely below — every living thing is tied to the soil, water, sunlight, and creatures around it.
points: How might the loss of forest cover and changes in rainfall lead elephants to enter human farms and villages?
Imagine you are a tree in a dense forest — what relationships would you have with water, sunlight, and other animals?
Can the Earth thrive without humans? Can humans survive without the Earth?

slides.title: A chain of events ties nature together
slides.body: In Odisha, Jharkhand, Assam, and other states, elephants enter farms when waterholes **dry up** and food grows scarce. Cutting trees for roads and buildings shrinks forests, so animals move into human areas. Wildlife ecologists mark **corridors** that let animals travel safely between forests — showing how closely nature's elements are connected.

slides.title: How do we experience and interpret our surroundings?
slides.intro: Different habitats hold different living and non-living things. Let us explore two nearby habitats and sort what we find.

slides.title: A habitat is where an organism lives
slides.body: A **habitat** is simply the place where an organism lives — it could even be just the **bark of a tree**. The plants and animals in it interact with each other and adapt to survive in the surrounding conditions. To understand a habitat, we explore it and identify both the living and the non-living parts.

slides.title: Explore a pond and a forest
slides.purpose: Do different habitats hold different things? We compare two nearby habitats to see what **living** and **non-living** components each one has.
steps: Identify — two habitats nearby, such as a pond, a forest, a farm, or a banyan, mango, or pilkhan tree
List — the living beings you observe in each habitat
Record — the non-living things too, in your own table
slides.observe: Both habitats hold **living beings and non-living things**, but the kinds differ. The living beings are the **biotic** components; the non-living things are the **abiotic** components — and every organism needs specific conditions to survive.

slides.title: Same idea, different components
A habitat supplies biotic and abiotic needs
slides.body: A pond gives fish **food, oxygen, shelter, and space**. Fish meet their **biotic** needs — food from small plants and animals — and their **abiotic** needs, such as oxygen, from water. Different organisms use the same habitat differently: a snake out at night and a rodent active by day share one habitat yet face different conditions. This is how organisms coexist in **harmony**.

slides.title: Who all live together in nature?
slides.intro: You rarely see just one fish in a pond. From a single kind to a whole community — let us count and name the groups.

slides.title: Count the organisms in one square metre
slides.purpose: How many of one kind live together? We count organisms in a fixed patch to understand the idea of a **population**.
steps: Mark — a 1 m × 1 m area in your school garden
Identify — any four organisms, plants or animals, in this area
Count — the number of each, and compile the data from all groups
slides.observe: You might find **20** of one plant but only **5** of another in the same area. A group of the **same kind** of organism living together at a given place and time is a **population**.

slides.title: From one population to a whole community
slides.body: The garden patch held **20** of one plant but only **5** of another — each group of one kind, living together at one place and time, is a **population**. But could a habitat hold just one kind? They would all need the same food, water, and space, and **compete** until resources ran short. So habitats hold many populations side by side — plants, animals, and microorganisms sharing one place form a **community**. Within it, organisms **interact and depend on one another** to survive: this interdependence is what 'living together' really means.

slides.title: Does every organism in a community matter?
slides.intro: What happens if one kind of organism changes in number? A study of ponds with and without fish gives a surprising answer.

slides.title: Ponds with fish, ponds without
slides.purpose: Does the number of fish in a pond affect plants on land? We read a real study comparing **Pond A (with fish)** and **Pond B (without fish)** to trace the ripples.
steps: Compare — the number of dragonflies, bees, and butterflies in both ponds
Relate — the number of dragonflies to the number of bees and butterflies
Think — about how the population of fish could affect seed production in nearby plants
slides.observe: Pond A (with fish) had **fewer dragonflies** — fish eat dragonfly **larvae**. Fewer dragonflies meant more **bees, flies, and butterflies**, which pollinate flowers, so plants near ponds with fish made **more seeds**. One change ripples outward.

slides.title: One organism's effect ripples through the web
slides.body: Fish eating dragonfly larvae is a **direct** effect; fewer dragonflies leading to more pollinators and more seeds in **St. John's wort** is an **indirect** effect. The study shows how **biotic** components — fish, dragonflies, pollinators, plants — and **abiotic** components — temperature, water, nutrients — affect one another. Could overfishing by humans upset this same balance?

slides.title: What are the different types of interactions among organisms and their surroundings?
slides.intro: Living things depend on non-living things, and on each other. Let us name the kinds of interactions inside a habitat.

slides.kicker: ACTIVITY 12.4 · LET US RELATE AND IDENTIFY
slides.title: Spot three kinds of interaction
slides.purpose: How do parts of a habitat affect each other? We use three criteria to **identify and describe** the interactions in a pond scene.
steps: Criterion 1 — interactions between biotic and abiotic components (an earthworm lives in moist soil)
Criterion 2 — interactions between two abiotic components (sunlight makes water evaporate fast)
Criterion 3 — interactions among biotic components (a frog eats insects; a water snake eats fish)
slides.observe: Interactions run **both ways**: between living and non-living parts, between two non-living parts, and among living things. Both kinds matter for survival in any habitat.

slides.title: Ecosystems — when components interact
slides.intro: Pull the interactions together and an ecosystem emerges. Some are watery, some on land, some made by us.

slides.title: Biotic and abiotic parts make an ecosystem
slides.body: When biotic components — plants, animals, microorganisms — and abiotic components — air, water, soil, sunlight, temperature — interact in a habitat, they form an **ecosystem**. **Aquatic** ecosystems include ponds, rivers, and lakes; **terrestrial** ones include forests, grasslands, and farms — even a single large tree. A farm is a **human-made ecosystem**.

slides.title: What does each organism eat?
slides.purpose: How can we sort organisms by how they feed? We study a forest scene and classify each organism by its **eating habit**.
steps: Spot — organisms like deer, hare, vulture, Bengal fox, shikra, squirrel, mouse, mushroom, and tree
Find out — what each one eats, using the library or internet
Record — whether each feeds only on plants, only on animals, or on both
slides.observe: Plants make their **own food** by photosynthesis, so they are **producers** or **autotrophs** (auto = self, troph = food). Organisms that depend on others for food are **consumers** or **heterotrophs** (hetero = other).

slides.title: Roles organisms play
rows: Makes its own food by photosynthesis

slides.title: Who eats whom — food chains
slides.intro: Link the feeding relationships and you get a sequence. Where does the energy in every food chain begin?

slides.title: Build a grassland food chain
slides.purpose: How are feeding relationships linked? We arrange grassland organisms into a chain to show **who eats whom**.
steps: Consider — grass, grasshopper, frog, hare, snake, and eagle in a grassland
Draw — arrows from each organism to the one that eats it
Read — one chain that results: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle
slides.observe: A **food chain** is a simple sequence showing 'who eats whom' in an ecosystem. It starts with **producers** that capture the Sun's energy; every consumer above them depends on it.

slides.title: Energy passes along, starting with the Sun
slides.body: Each organism in a food chain holds a specific position called a **trophic level** (troph = food). **Producers** like green plants are the first level; **herbivores** the second; **small carnivores** the third; and **large carnivores** the next. Energy flows up the chain, starting with the **Sun** — and the numbers shrink at each level, so a chain like millet → mouse → eagle stacks into a **pyramid**.

slides.title: Trophic levels form a pyramid
slides.caption: Each organism holds a position called a trophic level. Numbers shrink as you climb — many producers at the base, few large carnivores at the top.

slides.kicker: ACTIVITY 12.8 · LET US TRACE AND LINK
slides.title: Link the chains into a web
slides.purpose: Are food chains separate? We add the missing 'who eats whom' arrows to see how chains connect.
steps: Look — at grasses, hare, mouse, frog, grasshopper, fox, owl, bird, hawk, and snake
Add — arrows for every feeding relationship you can find
Notice — that each organism may be eaten by two or more others
slides.observe: Because each organism can be eaten by **several** others, the food chains interlink to form a network called a **food web**.

slides.title: What happens to waste in nature?
slides.intro: Organisms grow, function, and die, producing dead matter and waste. Who clears it away — and where does it go?

slides.title: Decomposers recycle everything
slides.body: Microorganisms like **fungi and bacteria** break down dead plants and animals into simpler substances, returning important **nutrients to the soil**. Mushrooms on dead wood and beetles on elephant dung do this work too. The process is **decomposition** and the organisms are **decomposers** or **saprotrophs** (sapro = rotten). In nature, nothing is wasted — everything is reused.

slides.title: How does one change lead to another?
slides.intro: A single small change can set off many more. Two real Indian examples show how far the ripples reach.

slides.title: Pollution in a pond, one step at a time
slides.body: Pollution makes pond **plants die**, so there is **less oxygen**, so **fish die**. With fewer fish eating them, **insects increase** and spread to nearby farms. Farmers then use **pesticides** to protect crops, which may harm the environment again — one change after another.

slides.title: The Indian bullfrog's warning
slides.purpose: What happens when humans intervene in nature? We read how exporting frog legs disturbed whole farms.
steps: Read — in the 1980s India exported frog legs of the Indian bullfrog (Hoplobatrachus tigerinus)
Trace — large-scale harvesting cut frog numbers, so pests rose, so farmers used more pesticides
Note — the Government of India banned the export to prevent further ecological damage
slides.observe: Since frogs eat insects, fewer frogs meant **more pests** and **more synthetic pesticides**, harming soil, water, and human health. An ecosystem stays in **balance** only when interactions keep populations and resources stable — a balance that is **dynamic, not fixed**.

slides.title: How do interactions maintain balance in ecosystems?
slides.intro: Besides eating one another, organisms compete and form partnerships. Both keep the ecosystem in check.

slides.title: Two ways organisms relate
slides.leftBody: Organisms compete for common resources — food, water, physical space, or sunlight. This competition controls population size and keeps the ecosystem balanced; without it, one species could multiply too much and cause imbalance.
slides.rightBody: Mutualism — both benefit (honeybees and flowers). Commensalism — one benefits, the other is unaffected (orchids on trees). Parasitism — one benefits, the other is harmed (ticks on dogs).

slides.title: What are the benefits of an ecosystem?
slides.intro: Ecosystems support our well-being — but we threaten them. The Sundarbans show both sides at once.

slides.title: The Sundarbans — gift and warning
slides.body: Forests give us **fresh air, fertile soil, food, fibres, timber, and medicines**; aquatic ecosystems give water and food. The **Sundarbans**, the world's largest mangrove forest, slow storm **winds and waves** and absorb carbon dioxide — a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987. Yet mangroves are cut for fuelwood, wildlife is hunted, and pollution damages the water, disrupting how the ecosystem works.

slides.title: Sustainable farming keeps the balance
slides.body: The **Green Revolution** of the mid-20th century used synthetic fertilisers and pesticides to end India's food crisis — but overusing them degrades **soil**, harms friendly microbes and natural predators, and lets pests resist. Growing one crop repeatedly, called **monoculture**, reduces biodiversity. Understanding ecosystems helps us adopt **organic and natural** farming that works with nature, not against it.

slides.title: How we harm ecosystems — and how we guard them
rows: Clearing forests for roads, farms, and buildings shrinks habitats
Loss of elephant corridors in Odisha, Assam
Waste in air, soil, and water poisons living things
Plastic and sewage in rivers and wetlands
A species brought from elsewhere that crowds out native ones
Taking more than nature can replace, like overfishing
Decline of the Indian bullfrog from over-harvesting
Land set aside to conserve habitats and rare species
Jim Corbett, Manas, Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve

slides.title: Nature works as one connected whole
slides.subtitle: From a pond's dragonflies to the Sundarbans' mangroves — every action ripples through the web of life. Protect the balance, and nature wastes nothing.
